transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Cora Vekulman, congressional Republicans are meeting
privately today to elect their new leadership teams, and Pia's Claudia Grisales has more.
Two top House Republicans are fighting to replace Speaker Mike Johnson as minority leader
of the incoming conference next year.
Johnson, who said he would step down after losing majority control, is staying out of
that and other leadership races, but he applauded those running.
Because we have extraordinary people who stepped up to lead in all these positions and tough
decisions ahead for everybody.
The number two House Republican, Steve Scalise, is running with a promise of scoring conservative
wins thanks to his broad experience in leadership.
He's facing off against House Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan, who says he'll provide
the kind of clarity for a path forward that has been missing under the current leadership
team.
Claudia Grisales, NPR News, the Capitol.
A new car now costs $51,000 on average.
That's a record, according to the Kelly Blue Book.
NPR's Willa Rubin reports on why cars have gotten so expensive and how people are actually
paying for them.
Every month, the Kelly Blue Book reports how much people paid for a new car in the previous
month.
They average the sticker price and add-on features for all kinds of vehicles, SUVs, pickup trucks,
electric vehicles, and from all kinds of companies, think Toyota, Subaru, Ford, Tesla, Mercedes-Benz.
It's a big average, but this average price is high.
A report from the auto analytics firm Edmunds also found new buyers are financing more than
ever taking out big loans and more than one in four financed with 84-month-long loan terms
last quarter.
Fast rates rising has also meant auto loans have gotten more expensive.
For new car buyers, it can all add up to a lot of sticker shock.
Willa Rubin, NPR News.
In Gaza, a grandmother survived a deadly landslide that buried several tents sheltering displaced
families during recent heavy rain.
As NPR's Anas Baba reports from Gaza, she says families knew the area was dangerous,
but they had nowhere else to go.
58-year-old Umel Abid Al Sahar was sleeping in her tent when the rain started.
Within minutes, the sand cliff above her collapsed, burying her and her daughter up to their wastes.
This survived, but the neighboring tents were completely swallowed by the mud.
From beneath the dirt, she screams for rescuers to save the family in its door.
Abu Salah, whose wife and children were among those buried, Sahar says displaced families
knew the cliffside wasn't safe, but had nowhere else to pitch their tents.
She says people throw themselves under mountains into the sea, anywhere they can find a place
to shelter.
Tell us where should we go?
Anas Baba, NPR News, Gaza.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is rejecting allegations filed against him yesterday in
impeachment articles in the House.
He held a press conference this morning.
He called the move a "political spectacle."
President Trump has repeated his strong support for Hegseth today.
The artificial intelligence company, Anthropic, has submitted documents for its initial public
offering.
The big tech firm will seek more than one and a third trillion dollars in the IPO.
The firm is expected to debut on Wall Street later this month.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
Postal workers unions are calling for the U.S. Postal Service to fully withdraw a plan
for future restrictions on mail-in voting.
As NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reports, the Trump administration may try to revive its push
for restrictions ahead of the 2028 election.
The Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration from using the U.S. Postal Service to carry
out mail-in voting restrictions for the midterm elections.
But the administration is still appealing a lower court ruling against the now blocked
ballot mail rule.
And it has a few more days to decide whether to appeal another ruling.
Both found USPS has no authority to refuse to deliver mail-in ballots in states where
election officials do not turn over their voter lists to the federal mailing agency.
Jonathan Smith is president of the American Postal Workers Union.
That is not the purpose of the Postal Service.
It is our job to deliver America's mail.
All their mail, not to determine who can vote and who can't vote.
Postal workers are picketing outside USPS headquarters and urging the agency's board
of governors to pull the ballot mail rule.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Congressional Republicans meet privately to elect new House leadership, with Scalise and Jordan competing for minority leader
Average new car price hits record $51,000 in Kelley Blue Book data, with more buyers taking long auto loans
Gaza grandmother survives landslide that buried displaced families' tents after heavy rain
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth rejects House impeachment articles as a political spectacle; Trump backs him
Anthropic files documents for initial public offering seeking over $1.3 trillion, expected to debut this month
Postal workers unions urge USPS to withdraw plan restricting mail-in ballot delivery for future elections
